text: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying to them:
Say to the Israelites: These are the creatures you may eat among all the animals on the earth.
Any animal that has a divided hoof, split in two, and that chews the cud—that you may eat.
But these you shall not eat among those that chew the cud or have divided hooves: the camel, because it chews the cud but does not have a divided hoof; it is unclean for you.
The rock badger, because it chews the cud but does not have a divided hoof; it is unclean for you.
The hare, because it chews the cud but does not have a divided hoof; it is unclean for you.
And the pig, because it has a divided hoof, split in two, but does not chew the cud; it is unclean for you.
You shall not eat their meat, and you shall not touch their carcasses; they are unclean for you.
Of all that lives in the water you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales, in the seas or in the streams—those you may eat.
But everything in the seas or streams that does not have fins and scales, among all the swarming creatures of the water and all the living creatures in the water—they are detestable to you.
They shall remain detestable to you. You shall not eat their meat, and you shall detest their carcasses.
Anything in the water that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you.
These are the birds you shall detest; they must not be eaten, for they are detestable: the eagle, the vulture, the black vulture,
the kite, and every kind of falcon,
every kind of raven,
the ostrich, the nighthawk, the gull, and every kind of hawk,
the little owl, the cormorant, the great owl,
the white owl, the desert owl, the osprey,
the stork, every kind of heron, the hoopoe, and the bat.
Every winged insect that walks on all fours is detestable to you.
Yet you may eat these among the winged insects that walk on all fours: those that have jointed legs above their feet for leaping on the ground.
Of these you may eat: every kind of locust, every kind of bald locust, every kind of cricket, and every kind of grasshopper.
But every other winged insect that has four feet is detestable to you.
By these you will make yourselves unclean: whoever touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,
and whoever carries any part of their carcasses must wash his clothes, and he will be unclean until evening.
Every animal that has a hoof but does not have it fully split, and does not chew the cud, is unclean for you; whoever touches them becomes unclean.

versions.text: Every animal that has a hoof but is not split in two, or does not chew the cud, is unclean for you; whoever touches them becomes unclean.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew joins the two conditions with the conjunction 'and' (וְגֵרָה אֵינֶנָּה מַעֲלָה): the animal is unclean because it both lacks a fully split hoof and fails to chew the cud. Rendering it 'or' turns two joint requirements into alternatives and would wrongly declare cud-chewing animals with split hooves unclean.

versions.text: Every animal that has hooves but is not split in two and does not chew the cud is unclean for you; whoever touches them becomes unclean.
versions.explanation: As written, the clause "but is not split in two" attaches grammatically to the animal rather than to its hoof, which is what the Hebrew (וְשֶׁסַע אֵינֶנָּה שֹׁסַעַת) says. Making the hoof the thing that is not fully split removes the dangling reference while preserving the joint 'and' condition established in the earlier revision.

text: Among the animals that walk on all fours, every one that walks on its paws is unclean for you; whoever touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,
and whoever carries their carcasses must wash his clothes, and he will be unclean until evening. They are unclean for you.
Among the creatures that swarm on the ground, these are unclean for you: the mole rat, the mouse, every kind of large lizard,
the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the skink, and the chameleon.
These are unclean for you among all the swarming creatures. Whoever touches them when they are dead will be unclean until evening.

Anything one of them falls on when it is dead becomes unclean—any article of wood, clothing, leather, or sackcloth, any utensil used for work. It must be put in water, and it will be unclean until evening; then it will be clean.
If one of them falls into a clay pot, everything in it becomes unclean, and you must break the pot.
Any food that may be eaten becomes unclean if such water has come on it, and any liquid that may be drunk becomes unclean in any such vessel.

versions.text: Any food that could be eaten becomes unclean if water from such a pot has touched it, and any liquid that could be drunk from such a vessel becomes unclean.
versions.explanation: The phrase 'from such a pot' adds detail not present in the Hebrew, which simply says 'on which water comes.' In the second clause the Hebrew places 'in any vessel' with the liquid, not as the source of drinking; the rewording keeps the sense while staying closer to the text and reading smoothly aloud.

text: Anything that one of their carcasses falls on becomes unclean; an oven or a cooking stove must be broken up. They are unclean, and they shall be unclean for you.
A spring or cistern holding water remains clean, but whoever touches one of these carcasses becomes unclean.
If one of their carcasses falls on any seed intended for sowing, the seed remains clean.
But if water has been put on the seed and one of their carcasses falls on it, it is unclean for you.
If an animal you are allowed to eat dies, whoever touches its carcass will be unclean until evening.
Whoever eats from its carcass must wash his clothes, and he will be unclean until evening; and whoever carries its carcass must wash his clothes, and he will be unclean until evening.
Every creature that swarms on the ground is detestable; it must not be eaten.
You shall not eat anything that moves on its belly, or that walks on all fours, or that has many feet—any creature that swarms on the ground—for they are detestable.
Do not make yourselves detestable with any creature that swarms. Do not make yourselves unclean by them, so that you become defiled through them.

versions.text: Do not defile yourselves with any swarming creature. Do not make yourselves unclean by them, or be made unclean through them.
versions.explanation: The verb שקץ ('make detestable') is rendered 'detest/detestable' throughout the chapter, so 'defile' here blurs the distinction between שקץ and טמא, which appear side by side in this verse. Keeping 'detestable' preserves the deliberate contrast.

text: For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves and be holy, for I am holy. Do not defile yourselves with any swarming creature that crawls on the ground.

versions.text: For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves and be holy, for I am holy. Do not make yourselves unclean by any creature that crawls on the ground.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם ("your souls/selves") with טמא is better rendered "defile yourselves," and הַשֶּׁרֶץ specifically denotes swarming creatures, a distinction the rest of the chapter maintains. "Unclean by" is also slightly awkward for oral reading.

text: For I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. Be holy, for I am holy.
This is the law concerning animals and birds, every living creature that moves through the water, and every creature that swarms on the ground,

versions.text: This is the law concerning animals and birds, every living creature that moves in the water, and every creature that swarms on the ground,
versions.explanation: Minor rhythm improvement for oral reading; "moves through the water" flows better and conveys the sense of הָרֹמֶשֶׂת בַּמָּיִם.

text: to distinguish between the unclean and the clean, between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten.

versions.text: to distinguish between the unclean and the clean, between the creatures that may be eaten and those that may not.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew repeats הַחַיָּה ("the living creature") in both clauses; the current translation compresses it and drops the repeated verb, weakening the deliberate parallelism that aids oral reading and memory.
